output.query: Hypoglycemia precipitating hepatic encephalopathy NASH cirrhosis mechanism

results.summary: Hypoglycemic episodes have been reported as a precipitant of encephalopathy in cirrhotic patients. Proposed mechanisms include glucose deprivation activating glutamine synthetase in astrocytes, and counter-regulatory hormonal responses impairing hepatic ammonia clearance. Case reports describe persistence of altered mental status after glucose normalization in cirrhotic patients with concurrent hyperammonemia.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 11) — precipitated by insulin-induced hypoglycemia event (glucose nadir 42) and skipped meal; persistent confusion after glucose correction reveals concurrent HE (ammonia 74).

differential.key_features: Glucose corrected but confusion persists — argues for a second pathology (HE) on top of resolved hypoglycemia.
Paracentesis if ascites; SBP often subtle in NASH cirrhotics.
CT head and exam without focal deficits exclude.
Clear iatrogenic insulin trigger (skipped meal + insulin); no need to pursue insulinoma.
Acidosis and glucose pattern would differ; not supported by current labs.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Hypoglycemia in NASH cirrhotics is dangerous and prolonged because hepatic gluconeogenesis is impaired; insulin regimens must account for liver disease.
Persistent confusion after glucose correction is a key signal that a second pathology (often HE) is present.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Glucose 42 caused the index event, but persistent confusion despite correction + ammonia 74 + NASH cirrhosis = concurrent HE that needs treatment.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all confusion to hypoglycemia and discharge once glucose normalizes.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Obesity is a NASH risk factor; the immediate precipitant is hypoglycemia + HE, not OSA.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue obesity-related causes (OSA, hypercapnia) as primary.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 44-year-old woman with NASH cirrhosis and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes who was brought to the emergency department by her husband after he found her confused at home while she was preparing dinner. He noted she was speaking incoherently, could not recognize him briefly, and appeared unsteady. She had taken her full basal insulin dose of 22 units the previous evening and her breakfast lispro dose of 6 units at 8 AM but then ate only a small snack rather than a full meal, having felt nauseous and without appetite since yesterday. Her glucose on arrival by EMS was 42 mg/dL, and she received oral glucose gel en route with partial improvement. In the ED, point-of-care glucose was 42 mg/dL and D50W was administered immediately. After glucose correction to 84 mg/dL over 30 minutes, her confusion persisted — she remained disoriented, slow, and had asterixis that appeared on exam 2 hours later.

neurological_exam.additional: Insulin pump NOT used — basal-bolus insulin regimen. Point of care glucose on arrival: 42 mg/dL. CRITICAL — hypoglycemia identified immediately. D50W 50 mL given. Repeat glucose 15 min: 68 mg/dL. Repeat glucose 30 min: 84 mg/dL. Mental status slightly improved but patient remains confused. Mild ascites on exam. No jaundice. No spider angiomata. NASH cirrhosis — no stigmata of chronic alcoholic liver disease.

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 (E4V4M5). Alert but confused — disoriented to time. Oriented to person and place. Slow to process questions. Asterixis absent on admission — prominent asterixis on arm extension on repeat exam 2 hours later. Number Connection Test 52 seconds (significantly elevated).
